title: ImageFlow — End-to-End DevOps Project
subtitle: A production-inspired DevOps OS with event-driven image pipeline, Terraform IaC, real k3s + Helm, dual-loop CI/CD, observability, and security hardening — built end-to-end on Floci for $0.
overview: Most DevOps tutorials teach isolated skills — 'here's how to write a Terraform module' or 'here's how to deploy to Kubernetes.' But production DevOps is about how all these pieces connect into a cohesive system. I wanted to build that system end-to-end.

ImageFlow is a production-grade DevOps platform built from scratch: an event-driven image processing pipeline with Terraform infrastructure, a real k3s Kubernetes cluster with Helm charts, dual-loop CI/CD (build + deploy), full observability with Prometheus and Grafana, and security hardening with network policies and secrets management.
The entire project runs on Floci (a free DevOps sandbox) for $0, proving that production-grade infrastructure patterns are accessible without enterprise budgets.
challenge: The Problem: The gap between DevOps tutorials and production reality is enormous. Tutorials teach tools in isolation; production requires understanding how Terraform, Kubernetes, Helm, CI/CD, observability, and security interconnect as a system.

I wanted to build a project that demonstrated end-to-end DevOps competency — not just 'I can write a Dockerfile,' but 'I can design, build, secure, observe, and operate a production-grade platform.' This meant covering infrastructure provisioning, container orchestration, deployment automation, monitoring, and security in one cohesive project.
The constraint was cost: I wanted to prove this could be done on a free tier, making it accessible as a learning resource.
solution: I designed ImageFlow as an event-driven image processing pipeline: users upload images via an API, which triggers a processing queue, which fans out to worker pods on Kubernetes for resizing, watermarking, and format conversion. Results are stored in S3 and served via CDN.

The infrastructure layer uses Terraform to provision all AWS resources: VPC, EKS-compatible networking (simulated on k3s), S3 buckets, IAM roles, and security groups. Every resource is tagged, parameterized, and follows least-privilege principles.

The Kubernetes layer runs on k3s (lightweight Kubernetes) with Helm charts for each microservice: API gateway, processing workers, monitoring stack, and secrets management. Network policies enforce pod-to-pod communication rules.

The CI/CD layer has two loops: the build loop (GitHub Actions builds Docker images, runs tests, pushes to registry) and the deploy loop (ArgoCD watches the Helm chart repo and syncs to the cluster). Both loops are fully automated with rollback capabilities.

architecture.heading: Event-Driven Pipeline
content: Image upload → API Gateway (nginx) → Processing Queue (Redis) → Worker Pods (k3s) → S3 Storage → CDN Distribution. Each stage is independently scalable and observable.

Workers are deployed as a Kubernetes Deployment with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, scaling based on queue depth. A failed image job is retried 3 times before being moved to a dead letter queue for manual inspection.

architecture.heading: Dual-Loop CI/CD
content: Build Loop: Push to main → GitHub Actions triggers → Docker build → Unit tests → Integration tests → Push to registry → Tag with commit SHA. Quality gates prevent broken images from reaching the registry.
Deploy Loop: ArgoCD detects new image tag in registry → Updates Helm values → Diff displayed in PR → Auto-merge after approval → Kubernetes rolling update → Health check → Promotion or rollback.

timeline.title: Infrastructure Foundation
timeline.description: Set up Floci environment. Built Terraform modules for VPC, networking, and IAM. Provisioned k3s cluster with initial configuration.

timeline.title: Application Layer
timeline.description: Built the image processing API and worker services in Python. Created Docker images. Set up Redis queue and S3 storage integration.

timeline.title: Kubernetes & Helm
timeline.description: Created Helm charts for all services. Configured deployments, services, ingress, and HPA. Implemented network policies for security.

timeline.title: CI/CD & Observability
timeline.description: Built GitHub Actions pipelines for build loop. Deployed ArgoCD for deploy loop. Set up Prometheus + Grafana monitoring stack.

timeline.title: Security Hardening
timeline.description: Implemented secrets management with Sealed Secrets. Added Pod Security Policies. Configured RBAC and network policies. Ran security audit.

learnings: Simulated production is still production. Running k3s instead of EKS didn't diminish the learning — the architectural patterns, Helm charts, network policies, and CI/CD loops are identical. The constraint of Floci's free tier forced creative problem-solving that enterprise budgets would have obscured.

Dual-loop CI/CD is the future. Separating build automation from deployment automation with ArgoCD watching a Helm chart repo gave us independent control over each loop. Builds could be fast and frequent; deploys could be deliberate and gated.

Observability from day one, not day 30. Adding Prometheus and Grafana in week 4 (not week 8) meant I could debug infrastructure issues during development, not just in production. This habit alone saved days of troubleshooting.

Security is not a layer, it's a dimension. Network policies, RBAC, secrets management, and Pod Security Policies aren't separate tasks — they're cross-cutting concerns that should be woven into every Terraform module and Helm chart from the start.
